Prototype for [#41](https://github.com/traitecoevo/austraits-means/issues/41) (`roadmap.md`, Later work). Render from the project root with `quarto render docs/local-range-model.qmd` after `Rscript R/scripts/run_location_prototype.R 50`. Functions in `R/model/local_range.R`.

## The question

The spatial product is, for a location and from its climate, the woody and non-woody **community mean** and **community range**: the spread of the species' trait means there (`terminology.md`). The pooled model has species effects only, so it pools every record from the same climate. The spread among its species then also includes how locations with the same climate differ, through soils or regional species pools. That overstates the range at any one location.

The location model adds a location effect, a 50 km equal-area cell with its variance per growth form, and a species × location effect:

```
log_value ~ 0 + g + g:(P_mn + T_mn + P_c + T_c)
          + diag(0 + g | taxon_name) + (0 + P_c | taxon_name) + (0 + T_c | taxon_name)
          + diag(0 + g | location) + (1 | taxon_name:location)
```

The location effect shifts every species of a growth form at a location together, so it does not spread them, and it is left out of the community range. The community variance of the species of growth form g at a location is:

- the spread of their fixed-effect predictions (they have different climate centres);
- plus the species variance of g;
- plus the species × location variance;
- plus the random-slope terms.

**Check.** For every location × growth form with at least five species, the observed variance of the species' mean log values, less the sampling term σ²/n, is compared with what each model implies for those same species. A ratio of 1 means the model gets the local spread right.

```{r setup}
source("R/init.R")
res <- readRDS("outputs/local_range/prototype_50km.rds")
res <- res[!vapply(res, is.null, logical(1))]
r2 <- function(d) dplyr::mutate(d, dplyr::across(where(is.double), ~ round(.x, 2)))
```

## Simulation

Simulated species of two growth forms are recorded at a few locations near their climate centre. The true variances are: species SD 0.4, location SD 0.4, species × location SD 0.15 and residual SD 0.2. In the first scenario species are placed independently of the location effect. In the second they *sort*: a species is more often recorded where the location effect is close to its own. Sorting makes co-occurring species more alike than species drawn at random, which the model's independence assumption cannot represent.

```{r simulation}
sim_check <- function(sorting) {
  sim <- simulate_location_data(sorting = sorting, seed = 1)
  old <- suppressMessages(fit_woodiness_model(sim$data, "sim", sim$groups, n_min = 0))
  new <- suppressMessages(fit_woodiness_model(sim$data, "sim", sim$groups, n_min = 0, location = "location"))
  vc <- tidy_varcomp(new)
  dplyr::bind_rows(
    `true variances` = summarise_community_benchmark(benchmark_community_variance(new, vc = sim$truth, noise_vc = sim$truth)),
    `location model` = summarise_community_benchmark(benchmark_community_variance(new, noise_vc = vc)),
    `pooled model` = summarise_community_benchmark(benchmark_community_variance(old, noise_vc = vc)),
    .id = "model") |>
    dplyr::mutate(scenario = if (sorting == 0) "independent" else "species sort among locations", .before = 1) |>
    dplyr::select(scenario, model, woodiness_group, n_locations, observed_community_sd, model_community_sd, ratio)
}
knitr::kable(r2(dplyr::bind_rows(sim_check(0), sim_check(3))))
```

With independent placement the location model recovers the local spread (ratio near 1); the pooled model overstates it by about half. With sorting, even the true variances overstate the local spread: the location model's assumption fails, and so it overstates it too, though by less than the pooled model. The real-data check below is what detects this.

## Diagnostic cells

For twelve 50 km cells per trait, spread along the rainfall gradient, preferring cells with both growth forms:

- each panel shows the trait records there (faint dots) and each species' mean of its records there (solid dots, sized by records);
- beside them are the modelled community mean and 90% range of species means for those same species, from the location model (solid) and the pooled model (dashed).

The location model's mean includes the cell's estimated location effect. That is why it follows the cell, whereas the pooled model's mean follows climate only. A range from climate alone (the product) would centre on the pooled model's mean, with the location model's width. The ranges are of species means, so the records spread wider than the bars by design.

```{r cells}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| results: asis
for (x in res) {
  if (is.null(x$diagnostics)) next
  cat("\n\n###", x$trait, "\n\n")
  print(plot_community_range_cells(x))
}
```

## Spread as a function of climate

The location model above has one species variance per growth form, so the community spread changes with climate only through:

- how far apart the climate centres of the co-occurring species are;
- the random slopes.

To let the species variance itself depend on climate, species are split into four classes by their climate centre (rainfall or temperature quartiles of the species, within each growth form). Each class gets its own variance: `diag(0 + spread_class | taxon_name)`. glmmTMB cannot make a random-effect variance a continuous function of a covariate, so this binned version is a test of whether spread varies with climate at all. A continuous version needs a hand-written model (RTMB, or Stan for the smaller traits).

### Continuous spread (RTMB)

The continuous version is written in RTMB (`R/model/spread_rtmb.R`), the same TMB engine and Laplace approximation glmmTMB uses, so likelihoods and AICs are comparable. For species s of growth form g, with standardised climate centre (p, t):

```
u_s ~ N(0, sd_u(s)^2),  log sd_u(s) = a_g + b1_g p + b2_g t + b3_g p^2 + b4_g t^2
```

Everything else is as in the location model. Two checks:

- With the climate terms removed, it reproduces the glmmTMB location model: same log-likelihood (to 1e-7 on LMA) and same variance components.
- On simulated data whose species SD rises with temperature, it recovers the slope and finds no rainfall effect (tests in `tests/testthat/test-local-range.R`).

### Shrinking the climate terms

Left free, the quadratic overfits groups with few species: non-woody seed mass (27 species) grows a hump to SD 2.5, and some curves fall to about 0 at the edge of the data. The climate coefficients b therefore get a prior, b ~ N(0, τ_d²), with one τ for the linear terms and one for the quadratic terms, shared by the two growth forms. τ is estimated from the data, so this is a ridge penalty with its strength chosen by marginal likelihood, as mgcv chooses smoothing parameters. A growth form that says little about how spread changes with climate is pulled toward constant spread, and a degree whose τ reaches 0 is dropped.

It is done as empirical Bayes in two steps:

1. From the free fit's coefficients b̂ and their covariance V, τ maximises N(b̂; 0, V + diag(τ²)).
2. The model is refitted with the penalty b²/(2τ²). That gives the posterior mode, its covariance (the curve bands) and an AIC with b counted at its effective degrees of freedom, on the same scale as the other AICs.

Integrating b inside the same Laplace approximation as the species effects was tried first and fails on real data. A species seen in only one cell can put its effect into the species × location term, leaving its species effect near 0. The joint density then grows without bound as that species' SD goes to 0, and the joint mode runs into this funnel.

Checks on simulated data (`tests/testthat/test-local-range.R`):

- with a real temperature slope, the slope survives and the null terms are pulled toward 0;
- with no climate effect, the linear τ goes to 0 and every coefficient to about 0;
- the refit agrees with the Gaussian approximation used to choose τ.

Each τ is estimated from only four coefficients, so it is noisy.

```{r spread-shrinkage}
purrr::map(res, function(x) if (!is.null(x$spread$shrunk)) {
  sh <- x$spread$shrunk$shrinkage
  tibble::tibble(trait = x$trait,
                 `tau, linear` = signif(sh$tau[["degree 1"]], 2),
                 `tau, quadratic` = signif(sh$tau[["degree 2"]], 2),
                 `terms kept` = paste(x$spread$shrunk$terms, collapse = ", "),
                 `effective df of b` = round(sh$edf, 1),
                 `log Bayes factor vs constant` = round(sh$log_bf, 1))
}) |> purrr::list_rbind() |> knitr::kable()
```

### Comparison

AIC relative to the location model with constant spread (negative favours spread by climate). The binned variants each add 6 parameters with both growth forms, the free continuous one 8, the shrunk one its effective degrees of freedom:

```{r spread-aic}
purrr::map(res, function(x) if (!is.null(x$spread)) tibble::tibble(
  trait = x$trait,
  `rainfall classes` = round(x$aic[["spread_precipitation"]] - x$aic[["location"]]),
  `temperature classes` = round(x$aic[["spread_temperature"]] - x$aic[["location"]]),
  continuous = if (!is.null(x$spread$continuous))
    round(x$aic[["spread_continuous"]] - x$aic[["location"]]) else NA_real_,
  `continuous, shrunk` = if (!is.null(x$spread$shrunk))
    round(x$aic[["spread_shrunk"]] - x$aic[["location"]]) else NA_real_)) |>
  purrr::list_rbind() |> knitr::kable()
```

Model-to-observed community SD ratio per growth form (as in the benchmark above; 1 is a match):

```{r spread-benchmark}
purrr::map(res, function(x) if (!is.null(x$spread$shrunk)) {
  loc <- dplyr::filter(x$benchmark, model == "location")
  tibble::tibble(trait = x$trait, woodiness_group = loc$woodiness_group,
                 `constant spread` = round(loc$ratio, 2),
                 free = round(x$spread$continuous$benchmark$ratio[
                   match(loc$woodiness_group, x$spread$continuous$benchmark$woodiness_group)], 2),
                 shrunk = round(x$spread$shrunk$benchmark$ratio[
                   match(loc$woodiness_group, x$spread$shrunk$benchmark$woodiness_group)], 2))
}) |> purrr::list_rbind() |> knitr::kable()
```

The species SD as a function of climate. The line and band show the shrunk continuous model with its 90% interval, with the other climate variable at the median species centre; the thin grey line is the free fit. Red points are the binned estimates, one per climate quartile of species; the dashed line is constant spread:

```{r spread-curves}

#| fig-height: 6

for (x in res) {

  cat("\n\n###", x$trait, "\n\n")

}
```

Species SD by climate class (natural-log units; class centre is the median centre of its species):

```{r spread-classes}
purrr::map(res, function(x) if (!is.null(x$spread)) purrr::map(x$spread, "classes") |>
  purrr::list_rbind() |> dplyr::mutate(trait = x$trait, .before = 1)) |>
  purrr::list_rbind() |>
  dplyr::mutate(cell = sprintf("%.2f (%s)", species_sd,
                               ifelse(by == "precipitation", paste0(round(climate), " mm"),
                                      paste0(round(climate, 1), " °C")))) |>
  dplyr::select(trait, by, woodiness_group, bin, cell) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = bin, names_prefix = "class ", values_from = cell) |>

```

Observed and modelled spread along each climate axis. Points are cells, coloured by how many species were recorded. The red line is the trend of the observed spread in cells with at least 10 species; the black lines are the trend of what each model implies for the same cells, and the green line the shrunk continuous model:

## Findings (runs of 24 and 25 November 2026)

Ratios below are corrected (3c2156f). An earlier version of this notebook left the species × location variance out of the location model's community SD, which made its ratios 0.03–0.06 too low.

- **The location model fits better for every trait.** All nine converge. AIC falls by 84 (leaf P per area) to 25,832 (height). Fits take seconds, except height: 6 minutes after the TMB 1.9.25 upgrade (19 before), for 320k records in 3,121 cells.
- **It removes most of the overstatement of the local spread.** Model-to-observed community SD ratios:
  - location model: 1.01–1.33 for every trait except wood density (1.57), mostly 1.10–1.25;
  - pooled model: 1.00–1.97.
  - The gain is largest for woody LMA (1.62 → 1.25), leaf P per mass (1.90 → 1.32), non-woody seed mass (1.44 → 1.01) and non-woody height (1.35 → 1.18).
  - Woody height was already about right under the pooled model (1.00; location model 1.10).
- **A residual overstatement of about 10–25% remains**, in the direction the simulation gives when co-occurring species are more alike than random. Two causes fit it:
  - real sorting, in which case the true local range is smaller than the model says;
  - studies measuring a few similar species together at a site, in which case the observed spread is too small and the model is closer to the truth.
- **The overstatement is concentrated in cells with few species, which points to the second cause.** Cells with 5–9 species give ratios of 1.16–1.95 (leaf P per area 3.19, from 9 cells); cells with 20 or more give 0.89–1.18. A sample variance does not shrink with the number of species, so the few species recorded together there are more alike than the cell's flora. Height, from herbarium specimens rather than targeted studies, is nearly flat (1.16 → 1.10). The diagnostic figures show the same: in wood density's cells with 5–8 species the species means cluster well inside the modelled range, while in its 51-species cell they fill it. Species-rich cells also differ in other ways (wetter, for one), so this is suggestive, not proof. Cell size barely matters between 10 and 50 km for LMA.
- **Spread depends on climate for some traits.** Against constant spread, the continuous model improves AIC for leaf area (−187), height (−91), wood density (−46) and seed mass (−27), but not for LMA or the leaf N and P traits. Where data are rich, the continuous and binned estimates agree:
  - woody leaf area: species SD falls from 2.35 at 10 °C to 0.60 at 27 °C;
  - woody seed mass: rises from 0.8 to 2.9 from cool to warm.
- **Free, the continuous model overfits small groups; shrinking the climate terms fixes that** (25 November).
  - Free: non-woody seed mass (27 species) gets a hump to SD 2.5 that the binned estimates do not show. Non-woody leaf P per mass and dry-end wood density go to about 0.
  - Shrunk: non-woody seed mass is close to flat (1.0–1.5), and its benchmark ratio returns from 1.24 to 1.01. Wood density becomes a smooth rise with rainfall and temperature that follows the binned points; its lowest SD is now 0.06 rather than 0. Non-woody leaf P per mass stays at 0.33–0.50.
  - Where the data are rich, shrinkage changes almost nothing: woody leaf area, woody seed mass, height.
  - The data choose the degree. The quadratic terms are dropped for seed mass, wood density and leaf N and P per area; the linear terms are dropped for LMA, leaf N per mass and leaf P per mass, leaving a slight quadratic. Both are kept for leaf area and height.
  - AIC against constant spread, shrunk: leaf area −190, height −93, wood density −43, seed mass −29, leaf P per mass −9, leaf N per area −6, LMA −4, leaf N per mass −1, leaf P per area 0. The free fit's +8 for leaf N per mass and +4 for leaf P per area disappear. Only the first four are clear wins (log Bayes factor 7–90; the rest 2 or less).
- **Against observed cells, climate-dependent spread is still mixed.** It helps wood density (1.57 → 1.38), woody seed mass (1.33 → 1.15) and non-woody height (1.18 → 1.13). It overshoots woody leaf area in cool and dry cells (ratio 1.23 → 1.43), while matching its warm, wet end. Shrinkage does not touch that, because those curves are well supported by the species data. Most of the cool and dry cells hold 5–9 species, the cells where the benchmark itself runs low.
- **The modelled species means move.** The SD of the change is 0.06–0.35 log units, with correlations of 0.85–1.00 between old and new. Height barely moves; non-woody LMA, leaf area and seed mass move most, because a species measured at one site no longer carries that site's effect.
- **Benchmark coverage decides which traits can be checked.** Plenty of cells for both growth forms: height (1,841 non-woody / 2,341 woody), LMA (36 / 167), leaf area (22 / 119). The other six traits have woody cells only, or fewer than 10 non-woody cells.

Not done yet:

- Predicting to a location from its climate alone. That needs the mean and spread of the climate centres of co-occurring species as a smooth function of climate, learned from GBIF co-occurrence; the benchmark above uses the species actually recorded at each location.
